analysis.one_liner: Requires annual conflict-of-interest disclosures for financial counselors who advise service members on bases.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the House Armed Services Committee, where it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten a law that already requires the Defense Department to use financially independent financial counselors on military installations. It would make that requirement mandatory rather than optional, require every counselor to file an annual financial disclosure with the Secretary, require the Secretary to review those disclosures for conflicts of interest, and bar conflicted counselors from advising service members until the conflict is resolved. It would also require annual reports to Congress on how many counselors were found conflict-free. The bill was never taken up by the House Armed Services Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and their families, who rely on Defense Department financial counselors for advice on loans, savings, and investments. The bill would make it harder for counselors with financial ties to the products they recommend — such as commissions from lenders or insurers — to advise troops, and would give Congress annual visibility into how many counselors are actually conflict-free.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that financial services be provided on military installations only through individuals who agree to submit annual financial disclosures to the Secretary of Defense.
Requires the Secretary to review every disclosure to confirm the counselor is free of conflicts of interest, and to bar any counselor with a conflict from providing services until it is resolved.
Requires annual reports to Congress on the percentage of counselors found free of conflicts, creating public accountability for the program.

analysis.who_pays: Financial services counselors and the firms that place them on military installations, who would have to file annual financial disclosures and could be barred from advising troops if they have a conflict of interest. Taxpayers would bear a modest administrative cost for the reviews and reports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Counselors and firms selling on bases

drawbacks.text: The bill addresses only conflicts of interest among counselors; it does not cap interest rates or ban any specific financial product, so a counselor could still lawfully recommend expensive loans after disclosing the conflict and being found otherwise free of it.

Annual financial disclosures and the requirement that conflicted counselors step aside until the conflict is resolved could shrink the pool of available counselors on installations, at least temporarily, if few counselors qualify as fully conflict-free.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: it targets a specific conflict — financial counselors who profit from the products they recommend to service members — using annual disclosures and a removal process, and adds congressional reporting to track compliance. The cost is modest: counseling providers must file annual disclosures, and any counselor with a conflict is barred from serving until it is resolved, which could temporarily reduce counseling availability. The honest objection is scope: this tightens conflict rules for counselors but does not itself ban or cap any predatory product, so its practical effect depends on how rigorously the Department of Defense reviews the disclosures.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee in April 2024 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 11, 2024, and referred to the House Committee on Armed Services the same day.
No further action was taken: it never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It had 13 cosponsors from both parties (8 Democrats and 5 Republicans), including members of both parties' leadership circles, but that bipartisan support was never tested in a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firms and individuals who sell financial products to service members on military installations are better off: the conflict-of-interest disclosure requirements they would have faced never became law, and no counselor they employ will have to file annual financial disclosures under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms selling to service members

for.name: Rep. Mikie Sherrill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require annual financial disclosures and conflict reviews for financial counselors serving service members.

for.name: 13 cosponsors (8 Democrats, 5 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, giving the bill backing from both parties, including Reps. Stefanik, Bacon, Gottheimer, and Davis.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 8 Democrats and 5 Republicans — so no vote ever revealed whether that balance would have held; the opposition was a silent one, the committee that never acted.

industries.industry: Consumer financial services firms serving military bases (payday and installment lenders, insurance and investment salespeople)
industries.note: Their personnel would have to file annual financial disclosures, and anyone with a conflict of interest could be barred from counseling service members on base. This narrows the channel through which commission-driven sales reach a captive audience of service members.
The people who would be better protected from conflicted financial advice on installations are themselves the intended beneficiaries, not an industry.
